attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack essay. He is not quoting anyone else.

semantics.note: 'Might happen' hedges the example scenarios, but 'would be even more risky' is a firm comparative under the antecedent 'if embedded in robots'. The normalisation keeps both the antecedent and the comparison with home assistants. The claim is close to a causal claim (embodiment raises risk), but treating it as a conditional forecast is acceptable.

contract.note: The plain reading (robot embodiment raises the likelihood or severity of harmful failures, compared with LLM home assistants) is ordinary and fair. Requiring comparative evidence, rather than robot hazards alone, matches the comparative wording. Marcus named no risk measure, so how risk is defined will decide the result.

evidence.note: Google's own 2023 announcement of RT-2, a model that directs robot actions. It shows the antecedent was met but says nothing about comparative risk, so it does not support the outcome.
A 2024 preprint showing jailbreaks that make LLM-controlled robots take harmful physical actions. It establishes a robot hazard but has no comparison with home assistants.

A Sept 2026 independent evaluation, published before the cutoff, finding that robot policies often carry out harmful instructions. It has no home-assistant comparison group and limits how far its results generalise.
A 2025 preprint showing a safeguard (RoboGuard) cuts unsafe robot plans from 92% to under 2.5%. Safeguards matter, but there is no comparison with assistants, so it does not contradict the claim.

reviews.rationale: The antecedent is met: RT-2 and later systems use LLMs to direct robots. But no item in the packet compares harmful-failure risk between LLM-controlled robots and comparable LLM home assistants. The robot hazard studies (e2, e3) and the safeguard result (e4) do not settle which way the risk difference runs. No deadline was stated, so the claim stays open.
